lenses.label: Application
lenses.about: The tiers of an application and the services that help them: who talks to whom.
lenses.not_drawn: Access policies, resource groups and tags. They define or restrict the roles above.

lenses.label: Network
lenses.about: How traffic reaches the application, and how administrators reach the servers. The shield is a set of filter rules on that hop.
lenses.not_drawn: Route tables and DNS records. They are settings on the roles above.

lenses.label: Infrastructure
lenses.about: What runs the code, and who it runs as.
lenses.not_drawn: Role assignments, resource groups and tags. They are settings on the roles above.

lenses.label: Security
lenses.about: Who can get in, what is checked on the way, where secrets are kept and where security events end up.
lenses.not_drawn: Role assignments and policies. They are settings on the roles above (see the Organization view).

lenses.label: Monitoring
lenses.about: How the application and its servers send logs, metrics and traces, and where they end up.
lenses.not_drawn: Diagnostic settings, alert rules and retention. They are settings on the roles above.
lenses.frame: Everything in here emits logs, metrics and traces

roles.name: Users
roles.what: People and systems that call the application, over the internet or a private network.
roles.where: The start of every request path.
roles.why: Everything else exists to serve them.
roles.note: A convention of the picture, not a service: no source applies.

roles.name: Edge (CDN/WAF)
roles.what: Caches content at a global edge and can filter malicious web requests with a web application firewall (WAF).
roles.where: In front of the load balancer, facing the internet.
roles.why: Absorbs load and blocks common attacks before they reach the servers.

az.name: Azure Front Door
az.note: Global edge entry with caching; a WAF can be attached.

az.name: Application Gateway with WAF
az.note: A regional layer 7 gateway; the WAF is a separate SKU (WAF_v2).

oss.name: ModSecurity
oss.note: WAF engine under OWASP custodianship; OWASP also maintains the Core Rule Set.

oss.name: Varnish
oss.note: HTTP accelerator and reverse caching proxy; a cache, not a WAF.

roles.name: Load balancer
roles.what: Spreads requests over several servers and stops sending to one that is unhealthy. Layer 4 balances TCP or UDP connections; layer 7 balances HTTP requests and can route by URL path or host header.
roles.where: Between the edge and the web servers.
roles.why: Servers can be added or replaced without clients noticing.

az.name: Azure Load Balancer
az.note: Layer 4, TCP and UDP.

az.name: Application Gateway
az.note: Layer 7, routes by URL path or host header. The load-balancing options page also lists TCP and TLS proxying.

oss.name: HAProxy
oss.note: Reverse proxy and load balancer for TCP and HTTP.

oss.name: NGINX
oss.note: Web server, reverse proxy and load balancer.

oss.name: Envoy
oss.note: Edge and service proxy; CNCF graduated.

roles.name: Web server
roles.what: Serves pages and static files, and passes dynamic requests to the application layer.
roles.where: First tier behind the load balancer.
roles.why: Keeps slow clients and static files away from the application code.

az.name: App Service
az.note: Runs web apps without managing the infrastructure. It also fills the application role.

oss.name: NGINX
oss.note: HTTP web server and reverse proxy.

oss.name: Apache HTTP Server
oss.note: Open source web server.

roles.note: The three tiers (web, application, data) are the common shape, taken as a judgement; many applications merge the first two.

roles.name: App service
roles.what: Runs the business logic. Talks to the data tier and to the side services.
roles.where: Second tier. Not reachable from the internet directly.
roles.why: The one place that decides what is allowed and what is stored.

az.name: App Service
az.note: Web apps, mobile back ends and APIs, without managing the infrastructure.

az.name: Container Apps
az.note: Serverless platform for containerized applications.

az.name: Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS)
az.note: Managed Kubernetes.

az.name: Virtual Machines
az.note: You manage the operating system and the software.

oss.name: Kubernetes
oss.note: Automates deployment, scaling and management of containerized applications; CNCF graduated.

roles.name: Database
roles.what: Stores structured data with transactions and a schema.
roles.where: Data tier. Reachable only from the application tier.
roles.why: The system of record: other stores hold copies.

az.name: Azure SQL Database
az.note: Fully managed; patching, backups and monitoring are handled.

az.name: Azure Database for PostgreSQL
az.note: Fully managed PostgreSQL (flexible server).

oss.name: PostgreSQL
oss.note: Open source object-relational database.

oss.name: MySQL
oss.note: Describes itself as the world's most popular open source database; the site is run by Oracle.

roles.name: DNS
roles.what: Turns a name such as app.example.com into an address. Azure has public zones and private zones that resolve names inside linked virtual networks.
roles.where: Off the request path: clients ask it first, then connect.
roles.why: Moving traffic means changing a record, not the application.

az.name: Azure DNS
az.note: Hosts public DNS domains and private zones.

az.name: Azure Private DNS
az.note: Name resolution for virtual networks linked to a private zone.

oss.name: BIND
oss.note: Name server software.

oss.name: CoreDNS
oss.note: DNS server in Go; CNCF graduated.

roles.name: Secrets store
roles.what: Keeps secrets, keys and certificates and hands them to the application on request, with access control and logging.
roles.where: Beside the application tier: the application asks for a secret, so it need not live in code or config.
roles.why: Secrets are managed in one place, and access can be logged.

az.name: Azure Key Vault
az.note: Callers sign in with Microsoft Entra ID; access uses Azure RBAC or a Key Vault access policy; logs can go to Azure Monitor.

oss.name: OpenBao
oss.note: Fork of HashiCorp Vault under the Linux Foundation (OpenSSF). Its licence is not stated on the page read: unconfirmed.

roles.name: Identity
roles.what: Signs users and services in and issues the tokens the application checks (OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect).
roles.where: Beside the application tier: the application calls out to it.
roles.why: Sign-in rules live in one place, not in every application.

az.name: Microsoft Entra ID
az.note: The Microsoft identity platform issues access, ID and refresh tokens.

oss.name: Keycloak
oss.note: Open source identity and access management; CNCF incubating.

roles.name: Message broker
roles.what: Holds messages between a sender and a receiver so they do not have to run at the same time.
roles.where: Beside the application tier. A sender puts messages in, a worker takes them out.
roles.why: Absorbs spikes, decouples services, and lets a failed job be retried.

az.name: Service Bus
az.note: Enterprise message broker with queues and publish-subscribe topics.

az.name: Event Hubs
az.note: Real-time streaming platform with an Apache Kafka endpoint (standard, premium and dedicated tiers).

az.name: Event Grid
az.note: Publish-subscribe for message distribution over MQTT and HTTP.

oss.name: RabbitMQ
oss.note: Messaging and streaming broker.

oss.name: Apache Kafka
oss.note: Describes itself as a distributed event streaming platform.

roles.note: Kafka is an event streaming platform, not a classic broker like RabbitMQ; it is often used in this role. Azure Event Hubs offers a Kafka endpoint, so Kafka clients can connect to it.

roles.name: Cache
roles.what: Keeps frequently read data in memory so the application does not ask the database every time.
roles.where: Close to the application.
roles.why: Lower latency and fewer database queries.

az.name: Azure Managed Redis
az.note: Current Azure service, based on Redis Enterprise software. Azure Cache for Redis retires: Enterprise tiers 2027-03-31, Basic, Standard and Premium 2028-09-30.

oss.name: Redis
oss.note: Redis 8 and later is offered under RSALv2, SSPLv1 or AGPLv3 (user's choice); 7.2 and earlier were BSD-3-Clause.

oss.name: Valkey
oss.note: BSD-licensed key/value datastore backed by the Linux Foundation.

oss.name: Memcached
oss.note: Distributed memory object caching system.

roles.note: Putting the cache in the same network segment as the application, for speed and to save network fees, is common advice. The Learn pages read do not state it, and state no general inter-zone charge: unconfirmed. Check your provider.

roles.name: Search
roles.what: A service for search over a copy of the data. Not the system of record.
roles.where: Beside the application tier, fed from the database or the broker.
roles.why: Databases are poor at free-text search; this is built for it.

az.name: Azure AI Search
az.note: Fully managed search service; full-text is one query type next to vector, hybrid and multimodal.

oss.name: Elasticsearch
oss.note: Distributed search and analytics engine.

oss.name: OpenSearch
oss.note: Open engine for search and observability, Apache 2.0.

roles.name: Worker
roles.what: Takes messages from the broker and does slow work outside the web request.
roles.where: Same tier as the application, behind the broker.
roles.why: The user is not kept waiting for slow jobs.

az.name: Azure Functions
az.note: Serverless, event-driven; scheduled tasks and queue processing.

az.name: Container Apps jobs
az.note: Containerized tasks that run for a finite time, on demand, on a schedule or on events.

oss.name: Celery
oss.note: Distributed task queue.

roles.name: Storage
roles.what: Keeps files that do not belong in a database: uploads, media, exports and backups. Object storage is reached over an API; file shares over SMB or NFS. A disk belongs to one server and is not drawn.
roles.where: Beside the application tier. The application and the workers read and write it.
roles.why: Cheap, large and shared; keeps the servers free of state.

az.name: Blob Storage
az.note: Object storage for unstructured data.

az.name: Azure Files
az.note: Managed file shares over SMB and NFS.

oss.name: MinIO
oss.note: S3-compatible object storage. Licence and project status are not stated on the page read: unconfirmed.

roles.note: Not in the mockup. Place and edges to be reviewed by the owner.

roles.name: VPN / link
roles.what: An encrypted tunnel, or a private connection through a provider, from an office or another network into the cloud network.
roles.where: At the edge of the private network (in the hub, in a hub-and-spoke design).
roles.why: Reach private services without exposing them to the internet.

az.name: VPN Gateway
az.note: Encrypted traffic between a virtual network and on-premises over the internet (IPsec/IKE).

az.name: ExpressRoute
az.note: A private connection through a provider that does not go over the public internet. The page does not say it is encrypted.

oss.name: WireGuard
oss.note: VPN; kernel components GPLv2.

oss.name: OpenVPN
oss.note: The page read does not describe it as open source: unconfirmed.

roles.name: Bastion
roles.what: A managed entry point for administrators: RDP and SSH to virtual machines over TLS, without a public address on the machines.
roles.where: In the hub (hub-and-spoke), reached over the VPN or the internet.
roles.why: Servers stay private: one door instead of an open SSH or RDP port on each.

az.name: Azure Bastion
az.note: The Basic and Standard SKUs need a public IP on the Bastion itself; Premium supports a private-only deployment.

oss.name: SSH jump host
oss.note: A pattern: a hardened server you connect through. No product page; no source.

roles.name: Firewall
roles.what: A stateful firewall service that allows or blocks traffic between networks by rules. It is a central service, not on every hop.
roles.where: In the hub (hub-and-spoke), as the main egress point. Whether inbound web traffic passes through it depends on the design.
roles.why: One place to see and control what crosses a boundary.

az.name: Azure Firewall
az.note: A fully stateful firewall as a service.

oss.name: pfSense
oss.note: Open source firewall; a commercial edition (pfSense Plus) also exists.

oss.name: OPNsense
oss.note: Open source firewall and routing platform.

roles.note: Architecture Center: with Application Gateway in parallel with the firewall, inbound web traffic goes straight to the servers and the firewall handles outbound and non-HTTP traffic; with the gateway in front of the firewall, traffic is routed through it. So a firewall on every hop is not the default. Bastion -> firewall -> server is not shown on the hub-and-spoke page: unconfirmed.

roles.name: Filter rules
roles.what: Allow and deny rules attached to a subnet or a network interface. Not a separate box: a setting that applies at network boundaries. Layer 3 and 4 only.
roles.where: On a subnet or a network interface, for example in front of the application servers.
roles.why: Each tier accepts only the traffic it expects.

az.name: Network security groups
az.note: Rules with a priority; applied to a subnet or a network interface.

oss.name: iptables / nftables
oss.note: Host firewall tools on Linux. No page was read: unconfirmed.

roles.note: Shown as a shield on the hops where filtering is typical. The Architecture Center says NSGs do not support FQDN rules and are less granular than a firewall for egress.

roles.name: Collector
roles.what: Runs next to the workload, gathers logs, metrics and traces, and forwards them.
roles.where: On each server or beside each container.
roles.why: The application does not need to know where telemetry ends up.

az.name: Azure Monitor Agent
az.note: Collects data from the guest OS of Azure and hybrid machines, governed by data collection rules.

oss.name: OpenTelemetry Collector
oss.note: Vendor-agnostic way to receive, process and export telemetry.

oss.name: Fluent Bit
oss.note: Telemetry agent for logs, metrics and traces.

roles.name: Telemetry store
roles.what: Keeps logs and metrics so they can be queried and alerted on.
roles.where: Central, outside the application servers.
roles.why: Evidence survives the server that produced it.

az.name: Azure Monitor Logs (Log Analytics workspace)
az.note: Log Analytics is the query tool; the data store is Azure Monitor Logs.

az.name: Azure Monitor metrics
az.note: Metrics store. The page for it was not read: unconfirmed.

oss.name: Prometheus
oss.note: Monitoring toolkit that stores metrics as time series.

oss.name: Grafana Loki
oss.note: Log stack; indexes labels, stores compressed chunks.

oss.name: Elasticsearch
oss.note: Also used as a log store.

roles.name: Dashboards
roles.what: Shows telemetry and notifies people when a rule trips.
roles.where: At the end of the monitoring path.
roles.why: Turns stored data into something a person can act on.

az.name: Azure Managed Grafana
az.note: Managed service built on Grafana for metrics, logs and traces.

az.name: Azure Monitor Workbooks
az.note: Interactive reports mixing text, log queries and metrics (reports, not dashboards as such).

az.name: Azure Monitor alerts
az.note: Alert rules on metric or log data that trigger action groups.

oss.name: Grafana
oss.note: Query, visualize, alert on and explore metrics, logs and traces.

oss.name: Kibana
oss.note: Explore and build dashboards on Elasticsearch data.

roles.name: SIEM
roles.what: Collects security events from many systems, correlates them, raises detections and supports investigation.
roles.where: Beside the telemetry store: it reads logs from the servers, the firewall and the identity provider.
roles.why: One place to look for an attack across all systems.

az.name: Microsoft Sentinel
az.note: Cloud-native SIEM; the page also describes SOAR capabilities.

az.name: Defender for Cloud
az.note: Cloud security posture and workload protection. Not a SIEM; listed because it feeds one.

oss.name: Wazuh
oss.note: Describes itself as open source XDR and SIEM.

oss.name: Security Onion
oss.note: Platform for threat hunting, network security monitoring and log management.

roles.note: Not in the mockup. Place and edges to be reviewed by the owner. The edge from the telemetry store is a judgement.

levels.about: The Microsoft Entra directory. The root management group has the tenant id as its id.
Group subscriptions; settings made here are inherited below.
Holds resource groups. All subscriptions in a management group trust the same tenant.
Holds resources that should share a lifecycle. Each resource is in one group.

org.what: The directory of users, groups and applications that sign-in is checked against.
org.why: The Identity role in the lenses is this, one level up.

org.what: Decides whether a sign-in is allowed from signals such as user, location, device and risk: block, grant, or grant with conditions.
org.why: Stops a stolen password from being enough.
org.note: That it is tenant-level is not stated in those words on the page read.

org.what: Time-based and approval-based activation of roles, for Microsoft Entra roles and Azure resource roles.
Rules about what may be deployed and how, checked against resources. A policy on a scope applies to everything below it.
org.why: Keeps every workload inside the same guard rails.
org.note: Assignment on a single resource is not stated on the pages read.

org.what: Who may do what, at management group, subscription, resource group or resource scope. Lower scopes inherit from higher ones.
org.why: Give access once, at the right level.

org.what: Costs and budgets at several scopes. Billing scopes depend on the agreement type, and management groups are not supported for every agreement.
org.note: Scopes vary by agreement (Enterprise Agreement, Microsoft Customer Agreement, CSP).

org.what: Cloud security posture and workload protection; the page says it is enabled on an Azure subscription.
org.why: One list of what to fix first.
org.note: Per-subscription plans and any management group option are not stated on the page read.

org.what: Records management (control-plane) operations: who created, changed or deleted what. Subscription events are the default view; tenant and management group scopes hold Resource Manager events only. Default retention 90 days.
org.why: The audit trail of the control plane.

org.what: Recommendations about cost, reliability, security and performance. The dashboard covers all your subscriptions and can be filtered.
org.why: A to-do list generated from your own estate.
org.note: Whether a recommendation is scoped to one resource, or to a management group, is not stated on the page read.

org.what: Every request from the portal, command line, SDKs and templates passes through it; it authenticates and authorizes them. Role-based access control is built into it.
org.why: Why Terraform, Bicep and the portal all follow the same rules.

org.what: Queries resources at scale across a set of subscriptions; the API also takes a management group.
org.why: Find things without opening each subscription.

org.what: A unified observability service for telemetry. Its Log Analytics workspaces are resources, so each sits in a resource group (the Resource Manager rule: every resource is in one group).
org.why: Why Monitoring appears in the lenses and here.
org.note: The workspace-in-a-resource-group point is an inference from the Resource Manager rule; the Monitor page does not say it.

org.what: A service with its own organization, connected to a Microsoft Entra directory for sign-in.
org.why: The pipelines that build into the resource groups.
org.note: That it sits outside the subscriptions is not stated on the page read; the Entra connection is.
